name: SmartAlbums
tagline: Desktop album design tool that turns a folder of client photos into print-ready wedding album spreads.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The core loop here is genuinely mechanical: read a folder of JPEGs, flow them onto spread templates, let the user swap and nudge, export pages at the right size with bleed. An agent can get you a working local version of that in a sitting or two, and for a photographer who only ever ships one album size it may be enough. What it will not get you is the long tail: hundreds of album manufacturer presets with their exact gutter and bleed quirks, color-managed output that the lab will not reject, client review links, and the fluid drag-and-drop feel that makes designing fifty spreads tolerable instead of miserable. Print is also unforgiving in a way web output is not, so the first album you order from your own PDF is the real test. Buildable, but the last ten percent is where the money is.
coreLoopDIY: Point it at a folder of photos, auto-flow them into spread layouts, rearrange and swap images by dragging, then export print-ready PDFs at a chosen trim size with bleed.
requirements: A folder of exported JPEGs (no RAW handling)
Exact trim, bleed and gutter specs from your album supplier
Willingness to order one test print before trusting the export
whatYouLose: Built-in presets for hundreds of album manufacturers and their spec quirks
Color-managed, lab-accepted output and soft proofing
Client proofing and revision rounds in a shareable gallery
Direct ordering handoff to print labs
The polish: snappy drag-drop, smart cropping, undo history, thousands of images without choking
moatNotes: The album supplier spec library plus lab ordering handoff is the part nobody wants to maintain themselves.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a photographer's billable hour is worth more than an evening of debugging bleed math, and because a rejected print order costs a client relationship. The tool is bought for speed and for the confidence that the PDF will come back as an actual album, not for the layout engine, which is conceptually simple. If you shoot one album size through one supplier forever, your own build is defensible. If you deal with several suppliers and clients who want revisions, the subscription is cheaper than the version of you that maintains a spec library.
notes: The layout engine is a weekend; the spec library and the lab relationship are not.
prompt:
Build a local-only album spread designer as a single project in this empty folder.

Stack, no substitutions: Vite + React + TypeScript for the UI, a small Node 20 Express server for file access, sharp for thumbnails, pdf-lib for export, plain CSS. No database, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Behavior:
1. On start, the server reads a photos directory path from .env (PHOTOS_DIR) and lists all .jpg/.jpeg/.png files. It generates cached thumbnails into .cache/ with sharp.
2. The UI shows a filmstrip of thumbnails on the left and a spread canvas on the right.
3. Album config panel: trim width, trim height, bleed in mm, gutter in mm, pages per spread fixed at 2. Store config in a project.json in the project folder.
4. Ship 8 hardcoded spread templates (1-up full bleed, 2-up, 3-up, 4-up grid, 1 large + 2 small, etc) defined as arrays of normalized rect coordinates.
5. Auto-flow: a button that takes all unplaced photos in filename order and fills spreads using templates, respecting photo orientation when choosing a template.
6. Drag a thumbnail onto a slot to replace it. Drag between slots to swap. Each slot supports pan and zoom of the image inside it with mouse drag and wheel, cropped to fill.
7. Spread list with reorder by drag, add spread, delete spread, duplicate spread.
8. Export: write one PDF per spread plus a combined PDF into ./export/, at full trim size + bleed, images placed at native resolution, 300 DPI target. Warn in the UI if a placed image falls below 200 effective DPI for its slot.
9. Autosave project.json on every change. Reopening the app restores the layout.

Out of scope, do not build: RAW decoding, ICC color management, client galleries, lab ordering, multi-user anything, mobile layout.

Include a README with setup steps, a .env.example with PHOTOS_DIR, and a loud note that the user must order a single test print before trusting the export for a real album.
